steps.body: Three-digit by one-digit division applies the same order every time: divide the place, write the digit, carry the leftover to the next place.
steps.narration: Three-digit by one-digit division applies the same order every time: divide the place, write the digit, carry the leftover to the next place.

widget.prompt: Check that 504 ÷ 6 = 84 by multiplying back: work 84 × 6.

commonResults.feedback: 484 stranded the carry out of the ones column, so the check falls ten short of 504.
That wrote only the ones-column product and never multiplied the tens place at all.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add column by column from the ones; when a column reaches 10 or more, trade and carry.
widget.successFeedback: 24,681 + 13,247 = 37,928 — the ones make 8 with a carry that the tens must include.

predict.prompt: Dividing 504 ÷ 6, can the hundreds be divided first?
predict.reveal: Five hundreds cannot make a group of six, so those hundreds join the tens and division begins there.

cml.actionGoal: Split a factor into places, build each piece, and reassemble the whole for g4m 3div1.
invariants: Splitting a factor never changes the product: every piece of the split multiplies the other factor, and the pieces add back to exactly the same total, which is what makes g4m 3div1 decomposable at all.
misconceptions: Adding only some of the partial products, dropping or inventing a zero when factors carry tens, or letting a remainder reach or exceed the divisor.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If one partial product were left out, exactly how much of the total would go missing?

commonErrors.feedback: That slid the quotient one place too far left — check which place the first digit belongs in.

widget.prompt: Dividing 936 ÷ 3, why do you start with the hundreds?

options.label: Because the largest place decides where the quotient begins
options.feedback: Correct — 9 hundreds split into 3 gives 3 hundreds, so the quotient starts in the hundreds place.

options.label: Because division always starts on the right
options.feedback: That is addition and subtraction. Division works from the LARGEST place downward.

options.label: Because 9 is the biggest digit
options.feedback: Its size is not the reason — its PLACE is. The leftmost place sets the quotient's first place.

options.label: It does not matter where you start
options.feedback: It does: starting elsewhere puts the quotient's digits in the wrong places entirely.
